More than 1.5 million | class = Compact [[sport utility vehicle]] | layout = [[Front-engine, rear-wheel-drive layout|Front engine]], [[rear-wheel drive]] / [[four-wheel drive]] | assembly = {{unbulleted list|United States: [[Toledo, Ohio]] ([[Toledo Complex]])|United States: [[Maywood, California]]||Argentina: [[Santa Isabel, Córdoba|Santa Isabel]] ([[Industrias Kaiser Argentina|IKA]])|Australia: [[Rocklea, Queensland]]|Brazil: [[São Bernardo do Campo]], [[São Paulo (state)|São Paulo]] (Willys Overland do Brasil S.A, later [[Ford Brasil]])|Canada: [[Brampton]], [[Ontario]] ([[Brampton Assembly (AMC)|Brampton Assembly]])|Egypt: [[Cairo]] (AAV)|Israel: [[Haifa]]|Israel: [[Nof HaGalil]] ([[Automotive Industries Ltd.|AIL]])|Iran: [[Tehran]] ([[Pars Khodro]])|Mexico: [[Toluca, Mexico State|Toluca]] (Willys Mexicana, later [[Vehículos Automotores Mexicanos|VAM]])|Spain: [[Zaragoza]] ([[Vehículos Industriales y Agrícolas, S.A|VIASA]])|Turkey: [[Istanbul]] (Türk-Willys Overland)}} | predecessor = {{unbulleted list| [[Willys MB]] (For World War II) | [[Jeep Commando]] (For pickup version) }} }} The '''Jeep CJ''' models are a series and a range of small, open-bodied [[off-road vehicle]]s and compact [[pickup truck]]s, built and sold by several successive incarnations of the [[Jeep]] [[automobile manufacturer|automobile marque]] from 1945 through 1986. The 1945 Willys "Universal Jeep" was the world's first mass-produced civilian [[four-wheel drive]] car. In 1944, [[Willys|Willys-Overland]], the primary manufacturer of the [[Willys MB|World War II military Jeep]], built prototypes for a commercial version – the CJ, short for "civilian Jeep".{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=zTsAbTJB5RIC&q=cj+jeep+stood+for+Civilian&pg=PA49 |pages=49–51 |title=Jeep Collector's Library |first=Jim |last=Allen |publisher=MBI Publishing |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-7603-1979-6 |access-date=22 May 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140708051243/http://books.google.com/books?id=zTsAbTJB5RIC&pg=PA49&dq=cj+jeep+stood+for+Civilian |archive-date=8 July 2014 |url-status = live}} The design was a direct evolution from the wartime Jeep, but the most obvious change was adding a tailgate, and relocating the spare wheel to the side. Also, besides adding basic civilian amenities and options and legally-compliant lighting, the CJ required a sturdier [[drivetrain]] than the wartime model, because the targeted rural buyers would expect years of durability, instead of mere weeks as during WWII. From then on, all CJ Jeeps consistently had a separate body and frame, rigid [[Solid axle|live axles]] with leaf springs both front and rear, a tapering nose design with flared fenders, and a fold-flat windshield, and could be driven without doors. Also, with few exceptions, they had part-time [[Jeep four-wheel-drive systems|four-wheel drive systems]], with the choice of high and low gearing, and open bodies with removable hard or soft tops. A few stand-out changes during 42 model years were the introductions of round-fendered vs. flat-fendered bodies (1955 CJ-5), straight-6 and V8 engines, automatic gearboxes, and different 4-wheel drive systems. The 1976 CJ-7 stretched the wheelbase by {{convert|10|in|cm}}, and made ''doors'' and a removable hardtop common items. After remaining in production through a range of model numbers and several corporate parents, the Jeep CJ line was officially ended after 1986. More than 1.5 million CJ Jeeps were built, having continued the same basic body style for 45 years since the Jeep first appeared.{{cite news |url= https://www.nytimes.com/1985/11/28/business/amc-to-end-jeep-cj-models.html |title=A.M.C. to End Jeep CJ Models |newspaper=The New York Times |date=28 November 1985 |access-date=13 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180314104411/https://www.nytimes.com/1985/11/28/business/amc-to-end-jeep-cj-models.html |archive-date=14 March 2018 |url-status = live}} Widely regarded as "America's workhorse", the CJs have been described as "probably the most successful utility vehicle ever made."{{cite book|last=Ackerson |first=Robert |title=Jeep CJ 1945-1986 |year=2005 |publisher=Veloce Publishing |isbn=9781904788966}} American Motors VP [[Joseph E. Cappy]] said the end of "CJ production will signal an end of a very important era in Jeep history."{{cite web |url= https://www.hemmings.com/blog/2011/02/18/class-of-86-jeep-cj-7-and-cj-8/ |title=Class of '86 – Jeep CJ-7 and CJ-8 |work=Hemmings Daily |first=Daniel |last=Strohl |date=18 February 2011 |access-date=13 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180113203036/https://www.hemmings.com/blog/2011/02/18/class-of-86-jeep-cj-7-and-cj-8/ |archive-date=13 January 2018 |url-status = live}} In 1987, the Jeep CJ-7 was replaced by the first-generation [[Jeep Wrangler]]. Looking very similar and riding on the same wheelbase as the CJ-7, it carried over some important components, including its use of [[leaf spring]]s. A similar model, the [[Jeep DJ|DJ]] "Dispatcher", was introduced in 1956 as a two-wheel drive version with open, fabric, or a closed steel body in both left- and right-hand drives for hotel, resort, police, and later [[United States Postal Service]] markets.{{cite book |last=Flory, Jr. |first=J. "Kelly" |title=American Cars, 1960-1972: Every Model, Year by Year |publisher=McFarland |year=2004 |pages=412, 700 |isbn=978-0-7864-1273-0}}{{cite book|last=Statham |first=Steve |title=Jeep Color History |date=1999 |publisher=MotorBooks International |isbn=9781610590556 |page=57 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=dR3wmKlfnrMC&q=Universal+rolled+out+of+Jeep+factories,+the+DJ-3A+Dispatcher.+The+DJ+series&pg=PA57 |access-date=13 March 2018}} ==CJ-1== {{Infobox automobile |name = Willys-Overland CJ-1 |production = 1944 |related = [[Willys MB]] }} In 1942, the [[United States Department of Agriculture|US Department of Agriculture]] tested the MB. By 1944, the Allies were confident the war would be won, and wartime production looked to be winding down. This allowed Willys to consider designing a Jeep for the postwar civilian market. Documentation is scarce, but in early 1944, Willys seemed to have found time to start drawing up plans, and one or two prototypes dubbed CJ(-1), for "Civilian Jeep", were running by May of that year. The first CJs had apparently been created by quick modification of the regular military MB, adding a tailgate, lower gearing, a [[Drawbar (haulage)|drawbar]], and a civilian-style canvas top. The first CJ served as a quick proof-of-concept test, and when a further design evolution materialized, it probably became the CJ-1 by default.{{cite web |url= http://www.fourwheeler.com/features/1507-the-oldest-restored-civilian-jeep/ |title=The Oldest Restored Civilian Jeep |last=Allen |first=Jim |date=27 July 2015 |website=FourWheeler.com |publisher=Extreme Ventures |access-date=13 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180222165444/http://www.fourwheeler.com/features/1507-the-oldest-restored-civilian-jeep/ |archive-date=22 February 2018 |url-status = live}} They were manufactured until the CJ-2s appeared, and they were the first Jeeps built from the ground up for civilian use. No CJ-1s built have survived, and how many were made is unknown.{{cite web |url= http://www.thecj2apage.com/story.html |title=The CJ2A Story |publisher=Thecj2apage.com |access-date=13 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171005221831/https://www.thecj2apage.com/story.html |archive-date=5 October 2017 |url-status = live}} {{clear}} ==CJ-2== {{Infobox automobile |name = Willys-Overland CJ-2 |production = {{unbulleted list|1944–1945|40 or 45 produced}} |engine = {{convert|134|CID|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Willys Go Devil engine|L134]] [[Inline 4|I4]] |transmission = 3-speed ''[[Borg-Warner T-90]]'' manual |wheelbase = {{convert|80|in|mm|0|abbr=on}}{{cite book|last=Gunnell |first=John A. |title=Standard Catalog of American Light-Duty Trucks |year=1993 |publisher=Krause Publications |isbn=0-87341-238-9}} |related = [[Willys MB]] }} Although at least 40 were built, the '''Willys-Overland CJ-2''' was not available for retail sale. The CJ-2s, also known as "AgriJeeps",{{cite web|last=Branch |first=Jon |date=2019-09-12 |title=A Brief History of the Jeep CJ Series - Everything You Need To Know |url= https://silodrome.com/history-jeep-cj/ |access-date=2020-10-21 |website=/silodrome.com}} were the second-generation prototypes for the first production civilian Jeep, and were used solely for testing purposes. Although their design was directly based on the military [[Willys MB]], using the same [[Willys Go Devil engine]], they were not only stripped of all military features, particularly the blackout lighting, but also the CJ-2s had many significant differences in body features and construction versus the military Jeep. They had tailgates, power take-offs, engine governors ($28.65), column-shift T90 [[manual transmission]]s, 5.38 gears, 2.43:1 low-range transfer cases, and driver's-side tool indentations. Rear wheelwells were redesigned so that seats could be enlarged, improved, and moved rearward, and new, more weather-tight top designs were tried. A canvas half-top with roll-down doors was one of several top designs tried before production. The CJ-2 Go-Devil L-head engine was largely the same as the wartime Jeep, but used a different carburetor and ignition system. {{citation needed span|text=The CJ-2s were built in two main batches, but even within the two groups, each was a little different, as they evolved and were modified for various types of work. For instance, several experimental combinations of powertrain components were tested. Earlier models were dubbed “pilot models” because they still had so many differences from the production Jeeps. They were painted olive-drab and had brass “JEEP” badges on the windshield base, the hood sides, and the rear. Some CJ-2s also had an "AgriJeep" plaque fixed to the dash.|date=June 2019}} Later models were stamped "JEEP" and were painted in a few civilian colors that translated into the "WILLYS" stamping and the colors that appeared on the first production CJ-2A Jeeps built from 1945. The spare tire was mounted forward of the passenger-side rear wheel on the earlier models and aft of the rear wheel on later ones. The CJ-2s were likely distributed to "agricultural stations" for evaluation purposes. Of the 40–45 CJ-2s built, serial numbers CJ2-03, CJ2-04, CJ2-06 (X30), CJ2-09 (X33), CJ2-11, CJ2-12, CJ2-14, CJ2-16, CJ2-26, CJ2-29, CJ2-32 (X56), CJ2-37 (X61), and CJ2-38 (X62){{Cite web |url=https://www.hemmings.com/stories/2019/09/29/hemmings-find-of-the-day-1945-willys-cj-2 |title=Hemmings Find of the Day – 1945 Willys CJ-2 |access-date=2020-09-27 |archive-date=2023-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230617030042/https://www.hemmings.com/stories/2019/09/29/hemmings-find-of-the-day-1945-willys-cj-2 |url-status=dead }} have survived, although some in very rough condition.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} CJ2-06 and CJ2-09 have been restored. {{clear}} ==CJ-2A== {{Infobox automobile |name = Willys-Overland CJ-2A |image = 1946 Willys CJ2A all original at 2019 AACA Hershey meet 1of5.jpg |production = {{unbulleted list|1945–1949|214,760 produced}} |transmission = 3-speed [[Borg-Warner T-90]] [[Manual transmission|manual]]{{cite book|last=Gunnell|first=John A. |title=Standard Catalog of American Light Duty Trucks, 1896-1986|year=1993 |publisher=Krause Publications |isbn=978-0-87341-238-4}} |engine = {{convert|134|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Willys Go Devil engine|L134]] [[Inline 4|I4]] |wheelbase = {{convert|80|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} {{cite web |url= http://www.oldcarbrochures.com/static/NA/Jeep/1949_Jeep/1949_Jeep_Universal_Operation_Data/1949%20Jeep%20Universal-20.html |title=1949 Jeep Universal Operation Data |publisher=Oldcarbrochures.com |access-date=2011-11-20 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120306064405/http://www.oldcarbrochures.com/static/NA/Jeep/1949_Jeep/1949_Jeep_Universal_Operation_Data/1949%20Jeep%20Universal-20.html |archive-date=2012-03-06 |url-status = live}} |length = {{convert|130.1|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} [https://www.kaiserwillys.com/about_willys_jeep_cj2a_history_specs About Willys Jeep CJ-2A - Jeep Specs and History | KaiserWillys.com] |width = {{convert|59|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} {{cite web|url= https://www.thecj2apage.com/specs.html |title=The CJ2A Page - Specifications |website=thecj2apage.com |access-date=2017-12-25 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171226020731/https://www.thecj2apage.com/specs.html |archive-date=2017-12-26|url-status = live}} |height = {{convert|69.4|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (top up) |weight = {{convert|2137|lb|kg|0|abbr=on}} }} [[File:1946 Willys CJ2A all original at 2019 AACA Hershey meet 4of5.jpg|left|thumb|1946 Willys CJ-2A interior]] [[File:'46 Jeep CJ (Auto classique Laval '10).jpg|thumb|1946 Jeep CJ|left]] [[File:1946 - Turner Motors - 31 Jan MC - Allentown PA.jpg|thumb|1946 advertisement marketed the "''Universal'' Jeep", not mentioning the CJ-2A type-code yet]] [[File:Jeeps voor landbouw en industrie, Bestanddeelnr 901-9334.jpg|thumb|Jeep demonstration for farming and industry – Netherlands, 1946]] The lessons learned with the CJ-2 led to the development of the first full-production CJ, the 1945-1949 '''Willys-Overland CJ-2A''', or '''Universal Jeep'''. A trademark for "AGRIJEEP" was granted in December 1944, but was not used. The CJ-2A looked very much like a civilianized MB with a tailgate and side-mounted spare wheel. A distinct difference between the MB and the CJ-2A lay in the grilles of the two vehicles. Where the MB had recessed headlights and nine-slot grilles, the CJ-2A had larger, slightly bulging headlights, flush-mounted in a seven-slot grille. While still powered by the reliable L-134 Go-Devil engine, the CJ-2A replaced the MB's T-84 transmission with a beefier T-90 three-speed. Production of the CJ-2A started on 17 July 1945, sharing production time with the MB roughly 9000 more MBs were produced through September 1945.{{cite web|url= https://www.thecj2apage.com/history.html |title=The CJ2A Page -- History of the CJ2A |website=thecj2apage.com |access-date=2018-05-06 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190524173858/https://www.thecj2apage.com/history.html|archive-date=2019-05-24|url-status = live}} Many of the early CJ-2As were produced using remaining stock of the military jeep components, such as engine blocks, and in a few cases, modified frames. Up to serial no. 13453, the MB-style full-floating rear axle was fitted. Once they were used up, the CJ got a stronger Dana / Spicer model 41. Sometimes the use of MB parts was due to strikes at suppliers, such as Autolite. Since Willys produced few parts in-house and relied heavily on suppliers, it was vulnerable to strikes. Unfortunately for Willys, strikes were common after the war, and this likely contributed to low production totals in 1945 and early 1946. Since the CJ-2A was primarily intended for farming, ranching, and industrial applications, stock CJ-2As only came with a driver seat and driver side mirror, and a wide variety of options was available, such as: front passenger seat, rear seat, center rear-view mirror, canvas top, front power take-off (PTO), rear PTO, belt pulley drive, capstan winch, governor, rear hydraulic lift, snow plow, welder, generator, mower, disc, front bumper weight, heavy-duty springs, dual vacuum windshield wipers (stock CJ-2As were equipped with a manual wiper on the passenger side and a vacuum wiper on the driver side), dual taillights (stock CJ-2As had a taillight on the driver side and a reflector on the passenger side), hot-climate radiator, driveshaft guards, heater, side steps, and radiator brush guard. The CJ-2As were produced in lively color combinations that in some ways symbolized the hope and promise of postwar America. True to their intended purpose, the combinations also resembled those used by the most popular farm equipment manufacturers of the day. From 1945 to mid-1946, CJ-2As were only available in two color combinations: Pasture Green with Autumn Yellow wheels and Harvest Tan with Sunset Red wheels. Additional color combinations added in mid-1946 were: Princeton Black with Harvard Red or Sunset Red wheels, Michigan Yellow with Pasture Green, Sunset Red or Americar Black wheels, Normandy Blue with Autumn Yellow or Sunset Red wheels, and Harvard Red with Autumn Yellow or Americar Black wheels. The Pasture Green and Harvest Tan combinations were dropped later in 1946. The Harvard Red combinations were dropped in 1947 and replaced with Picket Gray with Harvard Red wheels, and Luzon Red with Universal Beige wheels. In 1948, these color combinations were also added: Emerald Green with Universal Beige wheels, Potomac Gray with Harvard Red or American Black wheels. For 1949, the Picket Gray, Michigan Yellow, and Normandy Blue combinations were dropped. Olive drab was also available for export models. On early CJ-2As, the front seats were covered in olive-drab vinyl. Around mid-1947, Slate Gray vinyl became available for certain color combinations. Later, Barcelona Red was added to the mix. A total of 214,760 CJ-2As were produced. Because of the use of military production parts on the earliest CJ-2As, and the many changes made during their early production, restorers and collectors refer to CJ-2As up to around serial no. 34,530 as "Very Early Civilian" and from mid-1946 to about mid-1947 as "Early Civilian". Only minor changes were made after the mid-1947 models. {{clear}} ==CJ-3A== {{Infobox automobile |name = Willys-Overland CJ-3A |image = Willys mb 1943 06011701.jpg |production = {{unbulleted list|1949–1953| 131,843 produced}} |engine = {{convert|134|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Willys Go Devil engine|L134]] [[Inline 4|I4]] |transmission = 3-speed Borg-Warner ''[[Borg-Warner T-90|T-90]]'' manual |wheelbase = {{convert|80|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} |length = {{convert|129.8|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} {{cite web|url= https://www.kaiserwillys.com/about_willys_jeep_cj3a_history_specs |title=About Willys Vehicles - CJ-3A history specs |website=KaiserWillys.com |access-date=2019-10-30}} |width = {{convert|57.1|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (body) {{cite web|url= http://www.cj3a.info/index.html|title=The CJ3A Information Page |first=Bob |last=Westerman |website=cj3a.info |access-date=2017-12-25 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171225203206/http://www.cj3a.info/index.html |archive-date=2017-12-25|url-status = live}} /
{{convert|63.1|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} with spare tyre |height = {{convert|66.4|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} windshield up |related = [[Willys M38]] }} [[File:Jeep with plow attachment in 1949 ad art- Willys-Overland - Turner Motors - Matchbook cover- Allentown PA (cropped).jpg|left|thumb|Jeep with plow attachment in 1949 matchbook cover art]] The '''Willys-Overland CJ-3A''' was introduced in 1949, and was in production until 1953, when replaced by the CJ-3B. It was powered by Willys' {{convert|60|hp|kW PS|0|abbr=on}} L-134 Go-Devil four-cylinder engine, with a T-90 transmission and [[Dana Holding Corporation|Dana]] 18 transfer case, a [[Dana 30#Dana25|Dana 25]] front axle, and Dana 41 or 44 rear axle. It featured a one-piece windshield with a vent and wipers at the bottom. The CJ-3A had beefed-up suspension (10 leaf) to accommodate the various agricultural implements that were being built for the vehicle.{{cite web |url= http://www.film.queensu.ca/CJ3B/Siblings/CJ3AOrigins.html |last=Cary |first=Reed |title=The CJ-3A Universal Jeep |date=4 March 2001 |access-date=27 April 2013 |url-status = dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120626210611/http://www.film.queensu.ca/cj3b/Siblings/CJ3AOrigins.html |archive-date=26 June 2012 }} Another difference was a shorter rear wheelwell (the wheelwell from the top front edge to the rear of the body is {{convert|32|in|mm|abbr=on}} on the 3A compared to {{convert|34|in|mm|abbr=on}} on the 2A) and moving the driver's seat rearward.{{cite web|url= http://www.cj3a.info/cj3a/cj3a.htm|title=The CJ-3A| first=Bob |last=Westerman |website=cj3a.info |access-date=29 September 2008 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081006213747/http://www.cj3a.info/cj3a/cj3a.htm |archive-date=6 October 2008 |url-status = live}} As of 1951, a Farm Jeep and a Jeep Tractor version were offered; the latter was very bare-bones, for field use only, and featured a [[power takeoff]].{{cite web|url= http://www.cj3a.info/cj3a/farmjeep/fj.html |title=CJ-3A Farm Jeep and Jeep Tractor |first=Bob |last=Westerman |website=cj3a.info |access-date=2017-12-25 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171226130255/http://www.cj3a.info/cj3a/farmjeep/fj.html |archive-date=2017-12-26 |url-status = live}} In total, 131,843 CJ-3As were produced before the series ended in 1953. About 550 of the CJ3-As were assembled by [[Mitsubishi]] as the J1/J2 in late 1952 and early 1953, exclusively for the Japanese police and forestry agency.{{cite book|last=Ozeki |first=Kazuo |script-title=ja:日本のトラック・バス 1918~1972 |trans-title=Japanese Trucks and Buses 1918-1972 |publisher=Miki Press |year=2007 |page=131 |location=Tokyo |language= ja |isbn=978-4-89522-494-9}} [[File:Patent Case File No. 2,642,679, Ice Rink Resurfacing Machine, Inventor Frank J. Zamboni - NARA - 117724382 (page 87).jpg|thumb|left|Zamboni Model B ice resurfacer mounted on a Jeep CJ]] The CJ-3A-derived military jeep was the [[Willys M38|Willys MC (or M38)]], and it began complementing the Ford and Willys [[Willys MB|World War II jeeps]] starting in 1949. The CJ-3A, along with the later CJ-3B and CJ-5 models, was used as a platform for early [[Zamboni Company|Zamboni]] [[Ice resurfacer|ice resurfacers]] produced from 1950 until 1964, which were mounted on top of Jeeps to clean and smooth the surface of [[ice rinks]]. Zamboni resurfacer models produced from 1964 onwards have since been constructed using original chassis designs, eliminating the need to source Jeep parts.{{cite web|url= https://zamboni.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/EvolutionofZamboniMachine_web.pdf |title=Evolution of the Zamboni Ice Resurfacer |website=zamboni.com |date=2019 |access-date=September 21, 2023}}{{cite web|url= https://cj3b.info/Finds/FindsIce.html |title=More Unusual Photos: CJ-3Bs on Ice |website=cj3b.info |access-date=September 21, 2023}}{{cite web|url= http://www.ewillys.com/2017/03/06/zamboni%C2%AE-ice-resurfacers-the-jeep/ |title=Zamboni® Ice Resurfacers & the Jeep |website=ewillys.com |date=6 March 2017 |access-date=September 21, 2023}} {{clear}} ==CJ-4== {{Infobox automobile | name = Willys-Overland CJ-4 | production = {{unbulleted list|1951|One produced}} | engine = {{convert|134|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Willys Hurricane engine|Hurricane]] I4 | wheelbase = {{convert|81|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} }} The '''Willys-Overland CJ-4''' or "X-151" was only built as an experimental concept in 1950 or 1951.{{cite web|url= https://cj3b.info/CJ4.html |title=The Lost CJ-4 |website=cj3b.info |access-date=2017-12-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171011132938/http://cj3b.info/CJ4.html |archive-date=2017-10-11 |url-status = live}} It used the new [[Willys Hurricane engine]] and had an {{convert|81|in|mm|0|abbr=on|adj=on}} [[wheelbase]]. The CJ-4 body tub was an intermediate design between the straightforward raised hood of the CJ-3B and the all-new curved body style of the CJ-5. The design was rejected, and the vehicle was eventually sold to a factory employee.{{cite web |url= https://assets.hemmings.com/uimage/1364246-0-1200.jpg |title=Archived copy |access-date=2017-12-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171229112427/https://assets.hemmings.com/uimage/1364246-0-1200.jpg |archive-date=2017-12-29 |url-status = live}} Evidence has surfaced that derived prototypes called CJ-4M and CJ-4MA (XM170) have also been seriously considered, as precursors to the 1951 M38A1 and M170 military Jeeps. Although the CJ-4M prototype may not have been actually built,{{cite web|url= https://cj3b.info/CJ4M.html |title=The CJ-4M Jeep Prototype |website=cj3b.info |access-date=2017-12-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171011133113/http://cj3b.info/CJ4M.html |archive-date=2017-10-11 |url-status = live}} the stretched wheelbase ambulance prototype with registration "CJ-4MA-01" turned up in 2005.{{cite web|url= https://cj3b.info/CJ4MA01.html|title=CJ-4MA Jeep Prototype |website=cj3b.info |access-date=2017-12-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171011161927/http://cj3b.info/CJ4MA01.html |archive-date=2017-10-11 |url-status=live}} {{clear}} ==CJ-3B== {{Infobox automobile |name = Willys CJ-3B |image = Willyjeep01.jpg |related = Willys M606 |production = 1953–1968 |engine = {{convert|134|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} Hurricane I4 |wheelbase = {{convert|80|in|mm|0|abbr=on}}{{cite web |url= http://www.oldcarbrochures.com/static/NA/Jeep/1962_Jeep/1962_Jeep_CJ-3B_Brochure/1962%20Jeep%20CJ-3B-03.html |title=Jeep: 1962 Jeep CJ-3B Brochure |publisher=Oldcarbrochures.com |access-date=2011-11-20 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120306064326/http://www.oldcarbrochures.com/static/NA/Jeep/1962_Jeep/1962_Jeep_CJ-3B_Brochure/1962%20Jeep%20CJ-3B-03.html |archive-date=2012-03-06 |url-status = live}} |length = {{convert|129.875|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} }} The '''Willys CJ-3B''' replaced the [[#CJ-3A|CJ-3A]] in 1953, the same year Willys-Overland was bought by [[Kaiser Motors]]. The Kaiser parent company removed "Overland" from the Willys Motors subcompany name. The CJ-3B introduced a higher grille and hood to clear the new [[Willys Hurricane engine]]. A four-speed manual transmission became optional in 1963, at an extra cost of $194 (~${{Format price|{{Inflation|index=US|value=194|start_year=1963}}}} in {{Inflation/year|US}}). The turning radius was {{convert|17.5|ft|m|1|abbr=on}}.{{cite web |url= http://www.oldcarbrochures.com/static/NA/Jeep/1962_Jeep/1962_Jeep_CJ-3B_Brochure/1962%20Jeep%20CJ-3B-03.html |title=1962 Jeep CJ-3B (brochure) |website=oldcarbrochures.com |access-date=2012-05-31 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120306064326/http://www.oldcarbrochures.com/static/NA/Jeep/1962_Jeep/1962_Jeep_CJ-3B_Brochure/1962%20Jeep%20CJ-3B-03.html |archive-date=2012-03-06 |url-status=live}} Until 1968, about 196,000 CJ-3Bs were produced, of which 155,494 were assembled in the U.S.{{cite web|last=Redmond |first=Derek |title=Jeeps for Export |url= http://www.film.queensu.ca/cj3b/History.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20101205195030/http://www.film.queensu.ca/cj3b/Factory/FactoryExport.html |archive-date=2010-12-05 |url-status=dead |website=film.queensu.ca |date=2004-11-11 |access-date=2010-09-29}}{{cite web|url= https://www.kaiserwillys.com/about_willys_jeep_cj3b_history_specs|title=About Willys Vehicles - CJ-3B Universal |website=kaiserwillys.com |access-date=2017-12-27 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171228000138/https://www.kaiserwillys.com/about_willys_jeep_cj3b_history_specs |archive-date=2017-12-28 |url-status = live}} The CJ-3B was turned into the M606 military jeep (mostly used for export, through 1968) by equipping it with commercially available heavy-duty options, such as larger tires and springs, and by adding blackout lighting, [[olive drab]] paint, and a trailer hitch. Shipments of the M606 militarized version of the Jeep CJ-3B, exported for military aid under the [[Mutual Defense Assistance Act#Mutual Assistance Program|Mutual Defense Assistance Program]], accounted for a substantial percentage of the limited CJ-3B production in the 1960s. ===International licenses and derivatives=== {{See also|Mahindra Major}} The CJ-3B design was also licensed to several international manufacturers, which produced civilian and military variants long after 1968, including [[Mitsubishi Motors|Mitsubishi]] of [[Japan]] and [[Mahindra & Mahindra Limited|Mahindra]] of [[India]]. Mitsubishi's version was built from 1953 until 1998, while Mahindra continued to produce vehicles based on the Willys CJ-3B until October 1, 2010. The CJ-3B was also built by Türk Willys Overland in Tuzla County of Kocaeli city. It was the first off-road vehicle plant to be opened in [[Turkey]], in 1954. It was produced under ''Tuzla 1013'' brand.{{citation |title=1963 Türk Willys Overland: Universal Jeep CJ-3B |type=Museum placard |location=Hasköy, Istanbul, Turkey |work=Rahmi M. Koç Museum |quote=In 1954, the first off-road vehicle plant in Turkey, Türk Willys Overland Ltd., was founded by Mr. Ferruh Verdi.}} Mahindra's "Mahindra CJ" was produced in two versions: four-seater CJ 340 and six-seater CJ 540. Mitsubishi continued knock-down production of vehicles derived from the CJ-3B design until August 1998, when tighter emissions and safety standards finally made the Jeep obsolete. In total, about 200,000 units were built in these 45 years.{{cite web |url= http://www.mitsubishi-motors.com/corporate/ir/share/pdf/e/fact_2008.pdf |title=Facts & Figures 2008 |publisher=Mitsubishi Motors |page=40 |date=October 2008 |location=Tokyo, Japan |url-status = dead|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090320113933/http://www.mitsubishi-motors.com/corporate/ir/share/pdf/e/fact_2008.pdf |archive-date=2009-03-20 }} Short, medium, and long wheelbases were available, as well as a variety of bodystyles, and gasoline and diesel engines.{{cite web |last=Redmond |first=Derek |url= http://www.film.queensu.ca/Cj3b/World/Japan2.html |title=Jeeps in Japan |website=film.queensu.ca |date=2010-05-01 |access-date=2011-05-05 |url-status=dead|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110604024946/http://www.film.queensu.ca/Cj3b/World/Japan2.html |archive-date=2011-06-04 }} In Japan, it was sold at a specific retail chain called [[Mitsubishi Motors#Japan Sales Channels|Galant Shop]]. The Japanese GSDF refers to them as [[Type 73 light truck]]. [[File:Mitsubishi Jeep J-37 003.JPG|thumb|left|Mitsubishi Jeep delivery wagon J37]] The original J3 was a basic, doorless, and roofless version, with steering on the left, rather than the right, despite Japan having left-side traffic. The first right-hand drive versions did not appear until nearly eight years later (J3R/J11R). The original J3 and its derivatives were equipped with the {{convert|2199|cc|L|1|abbr=on|order=flip}} [[IOE engine|F-head]] "Hurricane" (called JH4 by Mitsubishi, for '''J'''apanese '''H'''urricane '''4'''-cylinder) inline four-cylinder, originally producing {{convert|70|PS|kW hp|0|abbr=on}} at 4,000 rpm.Ozeki, p. 140 In 1955, a slightly longer wheelbase '''J10''' which could seat six was added, and in 1956, the '''J11''' appeared, a two-door "delivery wagon" with a full metal body. This was considerably longer, at {{convert|433|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} versus {{convert|339|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} for the J3. Local production of the JH4 engine commenced in 1955. A locally developed diesel version ([[Mitsubishi KE engine|KE31]]) was introduced for the JC3 in 1958, originally with {{convert|56|PS|kW|0|abbr=on}} at 3,500 rpm but with {{convert|61|PS|kW hp|0|abbr=on}} at 3,600 rpm a few years later. Later versions used 4DR5 and 4DR6 (J23 turbo) 2.7 liter overhead-valve diesel engines. The final military version J24A produced 135PS from an improved 4DR5 engine with a front-mounted air-to-air intercooler. By 1962, the output of the gasoline JH4 engine had crept up to {{convert|76|PS|kW hp|0|abbr=on}}. By the time of the introduction of the longer '''J20''' in 1960, a six-seater like the J10, but with a differently configured (more permanent) front windshield, as well as available metal doors, Mitsubishi had also added small diagonal skirts to the leading edge of the Jeep's front fenders. This remained the last change to the sheetmetal up front until the end of Mitsubishi Jeep production in 1998. Later models include 2-L, short-wheelbase, soft-top '''J58''' ('''J54''' with a diesel engine), and the '''J38''' gasoline wagon on the longest wheelbase.{{cite book |ref=JAMA25 |title= 自動車ガイドブック |trans-title=Japanese Motor Vehicles Guide Book |language= ja |volume=25 |date=1978-10-10 |publisher =Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association |pages=206–207 |id=0053-780025-3400 }} The last iteration of the Japanese Jeeps was the J53 with diesel turbo engine. {{clear}} ==CJ-5== {{Infobox automobile | name = Willys CJ-5/Jeep CJ-5 | image = Jeep CJ-5 V6 red open body.jpg | production = 1954–1983

Power steering was an $81 option. The V6 engine proved so popular, by 1968, some 75% of CJ-5s were sold with it. [[File:Jeep-A-Trench on a CJ-5 rr.jpg|thumb|left|CJ-5 with the "Jeep-A-Trench" accessory]] Kaiser Jeep was sold to [[American Motors|American Motors Corporation]] (AMC) in 1970, and the Buick engine was retired after the 1971 model year. (GM's [[Buick]] division repurchased the engine tooling in the early 1970s, which served as the powerplant in several GM vehicles.) The "Trac-Lok" [[limited-slip differential]] replaced the "Powr-Lok" in 1971, and PTOs were no longer available after that year.{{cite web|url= http://www.jeep-cj.com/forums/f105/transfer-cases-12108/#post97071 |title=Transfer Cases - Jeep-CJ Forums |website=jeep-cj.com |access-date=2017-12-30 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171230225819/http://www.jeep-cj.com/forums/f105/transfer-cases-12108/#post97071 |archive-date=2017-12-30 |url-status = live}} AMC began marketing the Jeep less as a universal utility vehicle, and more as a sporty one, notably increasing its performance and features. '''1972 Revamp'''
The 1972 model year brought significant changes to the CJ-5. American Motors began fitting its own engines, which also required changes to both body and chassis. The base Willys 4-cylinder was replaced by AMC's Torque Command straight-6 engines, giving the entry-level CJ-5 the power of the previously optional Buick V6. Standard became the {{convert|232|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}}, and optional the {{convert|258|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}}, which was standard in California. Both engines used a one-barrel Carter YF carburetor. Also in 1972, [[AMC V8 engine#304|AMC's {{convert|304|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} V8]] engine became available, which upgraded the [[power-to-weight ratio]] to a level comparable to a V8 muscle-car. Other drive-train changes included a new front axle - a full-floating, open-knuckle [[Dana 30]], which was both 25 lbs lighter and reduced the turning circle by 6 ft. To accommodate the new engines, the wheelbase was stretched by {{convert|2.5|in|mm|0|abbr=on}}, and the fenders and hood were stretched by {{convert|5|in|mm|0|abbr=on}}.{{cite book |last=Cranswick |first=Marc |date=2011 |title=The Cars of American Motors: An Illustrated History |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=r9j7MWLE_jMC&q=1972+cj-5+nose&pg=PA241 |publisher=McFarland |page=241 |isbn=9780786485703 |access-date=2017-12-30 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171230231136/https://books.google.nl/books?id=r9j7MWLE_jMC&pg=PA241&lpg=PA241&dq=1972+cj-5+nose&source=bl&ots=tUrD5PeDip&sig=LbSTN4Sggq3bTVzuzxFl3cgocqw&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwichfjsg7LYAhWGmLQKHXwfBPg4ChDoAQhfMAk#v=onepage&q=1972%20cj-5%20nose&f=false |archive-date=2017-12-30 |url-status = live}}{{cite web|url= https://www.kaiserwillys.com/about_willys_jeep_cj5_history_specs |title=About Willys Vehicles - CJ-5, 6 |website=kaiserwillys.com |access-date=2017-12-30 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171230230454/https://www.kaiserwillys.com/about_willys_jeep_cj5_history_specs |archive-date=2017-12-30 |url-status = live}} A new box-frame was fitted, featuring six cross-members for more rigidity.{{cite web|url= http://www.classic-car-history.com/cj-jeep-history.htm|title=CJ Jeep History |first=Mark |last=Trotta |website=classic-car-history.com |access-date=2017-12-29 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171230114906/http://www.classic-car-history.com/cj-jeep-history.htm |archive-date=2017-12-30|url-status = live}} Also, a larger fuel tank was mounted, moved from under the driver's seat to under the rear, between the frame rails.{{cite web|url= http://www.jeepfan.com/tech/spotters-guide-to-the-72-75-amc-cj-5/ |title=Identifying a Jeep, An In-depth Spotters Guide to the 72-75 AMC Jeep CJ-5 |website=jeepfan.com |date=21 July 2009 |access-date=2017-12-30 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171230172559/http://www.jeepfan.com/tech/spotters-guide-to-the-72-75-amc-cj-5/ |archive-date=2017-12-30 |url-status = live}} A dealer-installed radio became available in 1973, and air conditioning became available via dealership in 1975. Electronic, breakerless distributors replaced breaker-point Delco distributors for the full engine line-up, and a catalytic converter was added to models equipped with the 304 V8.{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=zTsAbTJB5RIC&q=cj+jeep+stood+for+Civilian&pg=PA49 |pages=91–92 |title=Jeep Collector's Library |first=Jim |last=Allen |publisher=MBI Publishing |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-7603-1979-6 |access-date=22 May 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140708051243/http://books.google.com/books?id=zTsAbTJB5RIC&pg=PA49&dq=cj+jeep+stood+for+Civilian |archive-date=8 July 2014 |url-status = live}} In 1975, for the 1976 model year, the tub and frame were modified from earlier versions. The frame went from a partially open channel/boxed frame with riveted crossmembers, to majoritively boxed with welded crossmembers, and from parallel rails to widening fore to aft to benefit stability.{{cite web |url= https://www.jeep-cj.com/forums/f102/cj5-1972-1975-a-12408/ |title=Cj5 1972-1975 - Jeep-CJ Forums |access-date=2017-12-30 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171230172121/https://www.jeep-cj.com/forums/f102/cj5-1972-1975-a-12408/ |archive-date=2017-12-30 |url-status=live}} and the body tub became more rounded. The windshield frame and windshield angle were also changed, meaning that tops for the 1955 through 1975 model years are different from the 1976 through 1983 CJ-5 versions. The rear axle was also changed in 1976 from a [[Dana 44]] to an AMC-manufactured [[AMC 20|model 20]] that had a larger-diameter ring gear, but used a two-piece axleshaft/hub assembly instead of the one-piece design used in the Dana. For 1977, the frame was modified again to a completely boxed unit. Power disc brakes and the "Golden Eagle" package (which included a tachometer and clock) were new options, as well as air conditioning. In 1979, the standard engine became the {{convert|258|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} I6 that now featured a Carter BBD two-barrel [[carburetor]]. From 1980 through 1983, the CJ-5 came standard with a "Hurricane"-branded version of the [[General Motors|GM]] [[GM Iron Duke engine#Hurricane|Iron Duke]] I4 with an SR4 close-ratio, four-speed manual transmission. The {{convert|258|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} AMC straight-6 engine remained available as an option, but the transmission was changed from the Tremec T-150 three-speed to a Tremec T-176 close-ratio four-speed. The Dana 30 front axle was retained, but the locking hubs were changed to a five-bolt retaining pattern versus the older six-bolt. The demise of the AMC CJ5 model has been attributed to a December 1980 ''60 Minutes'' segment where the [[Insurance Institute for Highway Safety]] (IIHS) staged a demonstration to illustrate that the CJ5 was apt to roll over "in routine road circumstances at relatively low speeds." Years later, it was revealed that the testers only managed to achieve eight rollovers out of 435 runs through a corner. The IIHS requested the testers implement "vehicle loading" (hanging weights in the vehicle's corners inside the body, where they were not apparent to the camera) to generate worst-case conditions for stability.{{cite web|url= http://walterolson.com/articles/crashtests.html|title="It Didn't Start With Dateline NBC" (National Review 6/21/93)|first=Walter|last=Olson|website=walterolson.com|access-date=5 June 2017|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170512134539/http://walterolson.com/articles/crashtests.html|archive-date=12 May 2017|url-status = live}} ===Special CJ-5 versions=== *1961 '''Tuxedo Park''' *1962 '''Tuxedo Park Mark II''' *1963 '''Tuxedo Park Mark III''' *1964 '''Tuxedo Park Mark IV''' :The early Tuxedo Park models were trim lines designed to make the CJ "more comfortable and appealing to the general public."{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=zTsAbTJB5RIC&q=Jeep+Tuxedo+Park+Mark&pg=PA82 |page=82 |title=Jeep Collector's Library |first=Jim |last=Allen |publisher=Motorbooks |year=2004 |isbn=9780760319796 |access-date=9 December 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160603184045/https://books.google.com/books?id=zTsAbTJB5RIC&pg=PA82&dq=Jeep+Tuxedo+Park+Mark |archive-date=3 June 2016 |url-status=live}} However, the Tuxedo Park Mark IV was claimed as a separate model from the other CJ series (marked in 1965 as the "Universal"), with more differences than past models. In 1965, when the CJ was given the all-new Buick V6, Jeep saw the need for something similar in Australia. So, they began to fit [[Ford Falcon (Australia)|Australian Ford Falcon]] 6-cylinder engines to them at their Rocklea factory in Queensland. The Jeep was fitted with an engine, pedal box, and clutch/brake system corresponding to the equivalent Falcon at the time; a 1965 CJ5 would be fitted with 1965 Falcon engine/clutch components. Combat 6 jeeps were also fitted with Australian Borg Warner differentials and Borg Warner-brand gearboxes. Very little documentation about these Jeeps remains, and often the only way to conclusively identify them is by owner history.{{cite web|url= http://www.film.queensu.ca/cj3b/world/australia.html |title=Jeeps in Australia |publisher=The CJ3B Page |date=21 February 2012 |access-date=24 August 2012 |url-status = dead|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100716221723/http://www.film.queensu.ca/cj3b/World/Australia.html |archive-date=16 July 2010 }} ===Brazil=== [[File:Willys Jeep Universal 101 4p.jpg|thumb|1961 Willys Jeep 101 4 portas (aka "''Bernardão''")]] [[File:1963 Willys Jeep Universal.jpg|thumb|1963 Brazilian-built CJ-5]] While most foreign assemblers focused on the CJ-3B, Brazil received the CJ-5 instead. After having closed their market to imported cars in 1954, assembly of the "Willys Jeep Universal" (as it was known in Brazil) from CKD kits began in 1957. By 1958, production relied on locally sourced components, with the vehicles equipped with a {{convert|90|hp|kW|0|abbr=on}} 2.6 liter I6 engine (also used by Willys do Brasil for passenger cars). The Universals came with a three-speed manual transmission. The Brazilian-built vehicles are easily recognized by their squared-off rear wheel openings. In 1961, a long-wheelbase version, similar to the [[#CJ-6|CJ-6]], was added to the line. Called the "Willys Jeep 101", it shared the chassis of the local Rural, a redesigned [[Willys Jeep Station Wagon]]. Like the Brazilian-made CJ5s, the 101 has square rear-wheel openings. This version was introduced in 1961, but was not retained after Ford's takeover in the fall of 1967. On 9 October 1967, [[Ford do Brasil]] bought the Brazilian Willys subsidiary and took over the production of the CJ-5, the [[Willys Jeep Station Wagon]]-based "[[Ford Rural|Rural]]", and its pick-up truck version. Ford kept the line with no modifications except for some Ford badges on the sides and on the tailgate. In 1976, Ford equipped the CJ-5 and the Rural with the locally built version of the 2.3-L OHC four-cylinder engine used in the Ford Pinto (also used in the Brazilian [[Ford Maverick (Americas)|Maverick]]) and a four-speed manual transmission. This engine produced {{convert|91|PS|kW hp|0|abbr=on}} ([[Horsepower#Society of Automotive Engineers/SAE International|SAE]]) at 5000 rpm.{{cite book|title=World Cars 1981 |publisher=The Automobile Club of Italy/Herald Books |editor-last=Lösch |editor-first=Annamaria |page=259 |year=1981 |isbn=9780910714136 }} In 1980, the engine was modified to run on [[Common ethanol fuel mixtures#E100|Neat ethanol fuel]] (E100); this option lasted until 1983, when Ford ended the production of the CJ-5 in Brazil. {{clear}} ==CJ-6== {{Infobox automobile | image = Jeep CJ6.jpg | name = Willys CJ-6/Jeep CJ-6 | production = 1955–1981 | wheelbase = {{unbulleted list|{{convert|101|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (1955–1971)|{{convert|103.5|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} (1972–1981)}} | engine = {{unbulleted list|{{convert|134|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} Willys Hurricane I4|{{convert|225|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Buick V6 engine#Dauntless|Dauntless]] [[V6 engine|V6]]|{{convert|151|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} GM Iron Duke I4|{{convert|232|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} AMC I6|{{convert|258|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} AMC I6|{{convert|304|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[AMC V8 engine#304|AMC V8]]|{{convert|192|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} Perkins 4.192 I4 diesel}} | related = Willys M170 }} Introduced in 1953 as the military [[Willys M38A1#M170 ambulance|M170 jeep ambulance]], the civilian '''Willys Jeep CJ-6''' made its debut in 1955 as a 1956 model. It is a version of the CJ-5, stretched by {{convert|20|in|cm|0|abbr=on|adj=on}}, giving it a longer wheelbase of {{cvt|101|in|m|2}} from 1955 to 1971, and {{cvt|103.5|in|m|2}} from 1972 to 1981. The extended chassis allowed a variety of configurations, including adding a second row of seats. The M170 military version shared many of the features of the [[Willys M38A1|M38A1]] (Military CJ-5), but had the passenger-door opening extended back to the rear wheel well. As in the CJ-5, the V6 and V8 engine choices appeared in 1965 and 1972. The [[U.S. Forest Service]] also put CJ-6 Jeeps into use. American sales ended after 1975, with the introduction of the CJ-7. A total of 50,172 were produced when the series went out of production in 1981. Never very popular in the United States, most of CJ-6 production was exported to [[Sweden]] and South America. It was also assembled in South Africa, by [[Volkswagen]]'s local subsidiary,{{cite magazine |ref=SAM1076 |magazine=SA Motor |title=News Models |page=71 |editor-last=Howard |editor-first=Tony |publisher=Scott Publications |location=Cape Town, South Africa |date=October 1976 }} and in Israel, by Kaiser in [[Haifa]] and later by [[Automotive Industries Ltd.]] in [[Nazareth Illit|northern Nazareth]] (now [[Nof HaGalil]]).{{cite web|last=evyatar |title=ג'יפ ה"סיקס" הראשון |url= http://israelmotorindustry.org/jeep-cj-5-israel-1955/ |access-date=2021-08-16 |language=en-US}} In Brazil, a local 4-door option existed from 1961 to 1966 model years, called "Jeep Universal 101 Bernardão 4 portas". {{multiple image | align = left | width = 175 | image1 = Jeep M170 Ambulance sr.jpg | caption1 = M170, showing a larger opening that extends from the cowl back to the rear wheel. | image2 = 1975 Jeep CJ extended pumper fl.jpg | caption2 = 1975 Jeep CJ-6 fire engine, showing a smaller opening similar to other CJ models and shorter than on the M170. | image3 = 1979 Jeep-VIASA CJ-6 (6247698156).jpg | caption3 = 1979 Jeep-VIASA CJ-6, built with CJ-3B front end (Spain). }} {{clear}} ==CJ-5A and CJ-6A== {{Infobox automobile |name = CJ-5A & CJ-6A |production = 1964–1968 }} From 1964 until 1968, Kaiser elevated the Tuxedo Park from a trim package to a separate model for the CJ-5A and CJ-6A. A Tuxedo Park Mark IV is signified by a different prefix from a normal CJ-5, with a VIN prefix of 8322, and a CJ6a is 8422, while a normal CJ-5 VIN prefix is 8305 from 1964 through 1971. {{clear}} ==CJ-7== {{Redirect|CJ-7|the 2008 film|CJ7}} {{Infobox automobile | name = Jeep CJ-7 | image = 1980 Jeep CJ-7 blue V8 automatic Hershey 2012.jpg | model_years = 1976–1986 | engine = {{unbulleted list|{{convert|150|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[AMC Straight-4 engine|AMC I4]]|{{convert|151|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Iron Duke engine|''Iron Duke'' I4]]|{{convert|232|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} AMC I6|{{convert|258|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} AMC I6|{{convert|304|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[AMC V8 engine#304|AMC V8]]|{{convert|145|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} Isuzu [[List of Isuzu engines#Isuzu C engine|C240]] I4 diesel}} | transmission = {{unbulleted list|3-speed [[automatic transmission|automatic]]|3-speed manual|4-speed manual|5-speed manual}} | wheelbase = {{convert|93.3|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} | length = {{convert|148|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} | width = {{convert|68.5|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} | height = {{convert|67.7|in|mm|0|abbr=on}} | weight = {{convert|2707|lb|kg|0|abbr=on}}{{cite web |url= http://www.carfolio.com/specifications/models/car/?car=58366 |title=1979 Jeep CJ-7 car technical specifications |website=carfolio.com |access-date=21 April 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131102062433/http://www.carfolio.com/specifications/models/car/?car=58366 |archive-date=2 November 2013 |url-status=live}} | successor = [[Jeep Wrangler (YJ)|Jeep Wrangler YJ]] | related = [[SsangYong Korando#First generation (1982–1996)|SsangYong Korando]] }} The '''Jeep CJ-7''' had a wheelbase {{convert|10|in|cm}} longer than that of the [[#CJ-5|CJ-5]], with its curved side entry cutouts partially squared up to accommodate hinged doors. The other main difference between CJ-5 and CJ-7 was in the chassis, which consisted of two parallel longitudinal main C-section rails. To help improve vehicle handling and stability, the rear section of the chassis stepped out to allow the springs and shock absorbers to be mounted closer to the outside of the body. It was introduced for the 1976 model year, with a total of 379,299 built during eleven years of production. Transmission options included the standard part-time two-speed transfer case, automatic, and an optional new automatic [[all-wheel drive]] system called [[Jeep four-wheel-drive systems#Quadra-Trac|Quadra-Trac]]. Other features included an optional molded hardtop and steel doors. The CJ-7 was also available in Renegade and Laredo models. Distinguished by their different body decals, the Laredo model featured highback leather bucket seats, a tilting steering wheel, and a chrome package that included the bumpers, front grill cover, and side mirrors. An optional Trak-Lok rear differential was available, too. The final drive ratios of the CJ-7 were different for each type of engine: the {{convert|145|cuin|L|1|abbr=on}} [[Diesel engine|diesel]] was mated to the 4.10 ratio axle (in both Renegade and Laredo), while the {{convert|258|cuin|adj=on}} straight six and {{convert|150|cuin|adj=on}} four-cylinder used 3.73 and AMC V8 304-powered models (produced 1976–1981, which became part of the Golden Eagle version) used the 3.55 ratio axles. A diesel-powered version was made in the Ohio factory for export only. The engines were provided by General Motors, the owners of Isuzu Motor Cars. Production of this diesel version was between 1980 and 1982. This model had the Isuzu C240 engine, T176 transmission, and Dana 300 transfer case, although reports of some being produced with the Dana 20 exist. Typically, they had 4.1-ratio, narrow-track axles. From 1976 through 1980, the CJ-7 came equipped with a Dana 20 transfer case, Dana 30 front axle (27- or 31-spline), and a 29-spline AMC 20 rear axle, while in later years, Laredo packages added a tachometer, chrome bumpers, tow hooks, and interior upgrades including leather seats and a clock. In 1980, the Laredo was first fitted with an AMC 20 rear axle until mid-1986, when it was equipped with a Dana 44, and all 1980 and newer CJ-7s came with the Dana 300 transfer case. The Canadian Army took delivery of 195 militarized versions of the CJ-7 in 1985. These were put into service as a stop-gap measure between the retirement of the M38A1 and the introduction of the [[Volkswagen Iltis|Bombardier Iltis]]. They were codified by the Canadian Forces with the Equipment Configuration Code number 121526. The CJ-7 continues to be used in the sport of mud racing, with either the stock body or a fiberglass replica. CJ-7 has been successfully and widely used as a favorite for rock crawling, through simple and complex modifications. The Jeep CJ models are a series and a range of small, open-bodied off-road vehicles and compact pickup trucks, built and sold by several successive incarnations of the Jeep automobile marque from 1945 through 1986. The 1945 Willys "Universal Jeep" was the world's first mass-produced civilian four-wheel drive car.
In 1944, Willys-Overland, the primary manufacturer of the World War II military Jeep, built prototypes for a commercial version – the CJ, short for "civilian Jeep". The design was a direct evolution from the wartime Jeep, but the most obvious change was adding a tailgate, and relocating the spare wheel to the side. Also, besides adding basic civilian amenities and options and legally-compliant lighting, the CJ required a sturdier drivetrain than the wartime model, because the targeted rural buyers would expect years of durability, instead of mere weeks as during WWII.
From then on, all CJ Jeeps consistently had a separate body and frame, rigid live axles with leaf springs both front and rear, a tapering nose design with flared fenders, and a fold-flat windshield, and could be driven without doors. Also, with few exceptions, they had part-time four-wheel drive systems, with the choice of high and low gearing, and open bodies with removable hard or soft tops. A few stand-out changes during 42 model years were the introductions of round-fendered vs. flat-fendered bodies (1955 CJ-5), straight-6 and V8 engines, automatic gearboxes, and different 4-wheel drive systems. The 1976 CJ-7 stretched the wheelbase by 10 inches (25 cm), and made doors and a removable hardtop common items.
After remaining in production through a range of model numbers and several corporate parents, the Jeep CJ line was officially ended after 1986. More than 1.5 million CJ Jeeps were built, having continued the same basic body style for 45 years since the Jeep first appeared. Widely regarded as "America's workhorse", the CJs have been described as "probably the most successful utility vehicle ever made." American Motors VP Joseph E. Cappy said the end of "CJ production will signal an end of a very important era in Jeep history." In 1987, the Jeep CJ-7 was replaced by the first-generation Jeep Wrangler. Looking very similar and riding on the same wheelbase as the CJ-7, it carried over some important components, including its use of leaf springs.
A similar model, the DJ "Dispatcher", was introduced in 1956 as a two-wheel drive version with open, fabric, or a closed steel body in both left- and right-hand drives for hotel, resort, police, and later United States Postal Service markets.
